content: The credibility of guidelines can be compromised if the publication date, presentation, background text, evidence synthesis methods, or evidence-to-decision (EtD) considerations are outdated or unclear. Additionally, feedback from end-users may reveal recommendations that are conflicting, ambiguous, outdated, or difficult to implement, necessitating updates to the guidelines. The World Health Organization (WHO) global strategy to accelerate the elimination of cervical cancer, endorsed by Member States during the World Health Assembly in 2020, highlighted the urgent need for updated WHO guidance on cervical cancer screening and treatment. The previous WHO guidance, published in 2013, was deemed in need of revision to better support country-level decision-making for initiating and scaling up cervical cancer prevention programs. The process of updating the guideline began in 2019, incorporating implementation experiences and research findings. The updated recommendations were designed to be both feasible and acceptable for healthcare workers providing screening and treatment services, as well as for the end-users of these services. This guideline aims to support efforts to achieve the 2030 targets of the global strategy. The primary objective of the guideline is to enhance national strategies for cervical cancer screening and treatment, ensuring inclusivity for all women, including those living with HIV. The guideline development process was divided into four phases, with the current document presenting the outcomes of Phase 1. The updates include revised recommendations on screening and treatment strategies, clinical algorithms for commonly used approaches, and evidence evaluation for strategies not prioritized in Phase 1. Future phases will address implementation recommendations and establish a living guideline to allow for continuous updates as new evidence emerges. Since the publication of the 2013 guideline, significant advancements have been made. WHO has pre-qualified HPV screening tests, and thermal ablation and cryotherapy have been added as recommended ablative treatment methods. Some interventions from the 2013 guideline, such as cytology or histological diagnosis, may no longer be relevant or widely used in many countries. High-quality studies published in the intervening years have evaluated new tests, recurrence rates after treatment, and appropriate screening intervals. New data is also available regarding women living with HIV, including the type of screening and treatment and the recommended age to begin screening. The updated guideline also seeks to clarify the optimal number of lifetime screenings, the recommended age for the first screening, and the frequency of subsequent screenings following negative results or treatment for pre-cancer lesions. The target audience for this document includes policymakers, program managers, and healthcare professionals responsible for cervical cancer prevention strategies at various levels. It is also intended to inform women, girls, and their families about cervical cancer screening and treatment options. The guideline emphasizes the right to equality and non-discrimination in sexual and reproductive healthcare. It acknowledges that most evidence on cervical cancer is based on cisgender women but recognizes the need for cervical cancer prevention services for all individuals with a female reproductive system, including transgender men, non-binary, gender-fluid, and intersex individuals. For simplicity, the term women is used to refer to all gender-diverse individuals at risk for cervical cancer. Providers of sexual and reproductive health services must ensure equal care for all individuals, regardless of gender identity or expression. The updated guideline was developed following the methods outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The process involved contributions from various groups, including the Guideline Development Group (GDG), External Review Group (ERG), systematic review teams, and modeling teams. The GDG, established in 2019, reviewed the 2013 recommendations, prioritized key questions, and provided feedback on evidence reviews. The GDG consisted of 52 members with diverse expertise in cervical screening and treatment, representing all six WHO regions, civil society organizations, and women’s groups, including women living with HIV. The ERG, comprising 18 members with expertise in research, policy development, program implementation, and clinical care, reviewed the draft guideline and provided feedback. Multiple teams prepared evidence, including systematic reviews, mathematical models, and surveys on the feasibility of screening approaches and women’s values and preferences. The guideline development process included rigorous methods for evidence synthesis, following the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development and the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. A hierarchical approach was used to avoid duplication of reviews, starting with pre-existing systematic reviews and then searching for primary studies. The evidence was synthesized for each PICO question, addressing critical outcomes such as cervical cancer mortality, high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN2+), HPV infection, preterm birth, acceptability, adverse events, costs, feasibility, and equity. The guideline also prioritized seven screening and treatment algorithms, including screen-and-treat and screen-triage-and-treat approaches, using various combinations of primary screening tests (e.g., HPV DNA detection, cytology, VIA) and triage methods (e.g., colposcopy, HPV 16/18 genotyping). These algorithms were evaluated for their effectiveness and feasibility in different settings. The updated guideline aims to provide evidence-based recommendations to improve cervical cancer prevention strategies, ensuring inclusivity, equity, and feasibility for all individuals at risk.
